title: Cello Concerto in B minor
hook: Written by a homesick Dvořák in New York, for an instrument he had long thought unfit for a concerto.

painting.title: Birch Mood
painting.pairingNote: An autumn birch wood in Bohemia, painted two years after the concerto; the Czech countryside Dvořák longed for in New York and went home to in 1895.

facts: Dvořák wrote the concerto in New York between November 1894 and February 1895, in his last season as director of the National Conservatory. He was homesick and left for Bohemia soon after.

For years he had refused the cellist Hanuš Wihan’s requests for a concerto. He thought the cello fine in the orchestra but weak as a soloist, with a nasal top and a mumbling bass. Hearing Victor Herbert’s Second Cello Concerto in New York in 1894 changed his mind.

While he worked, his sister-in-law Josefina, his first love, wrote that she was seriously ill. He quoted her favourite of his songs, “Leave Me Alone”, in the slow movement. She died in May 1895, and he rewrote the end of the finale in her memory.

He refused to let anyone add a [[cadenza|cadenza]]. The finale, he wrote, should die away “like a breath” before the orchestra ends it stormily. The first performance was in London on 19 March 1896, with Leo Stern as soloist and Dvořák conducting.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a grand, singing [[sonata-form|sonata form]] with a famous horn tune (I), a tender song interrupted by grief (II), a march-like [[rondo|rondo]] that slows into a farewell (III).

movements.heading: Allegro
movements.summary: The orchestra plays both main themes before the cello enters: a quiet, brooding tune for clarinets and a long, tender melody for solo horn. Then the cello comes in with a bold flourish and takes over both themes. The movement ends in a blaze of B major.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 1, brooding
mainIdeas.description: a low, quiet tune for two clarinets, later played *grandioso* by the full orchestra.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 2, the horn tune
mainIdeas.description: a long, tender melody, first on a solo horn.

stops.hear: Clarinets play a quiet, brooding tune over low strings
The whole orchestra takes up the tune, loud and grand
A solo horn sings a long, tender melody
The cello enters with a strong, free flourish, then rich three-note chords
stops.happening: The soloist’s entry, *quasi improvisando*. Theme 1 now in B major

stops.hear: The cello races through the first theme in fast, brilliant figures
The cello sings the horn tune, softly and slowly
The orchestra bursts in loudly
The music becomes slow and dreamy; the cello plays Theme 1 softly in a distant key, with a flute
The whole orchestra plays the horn tune in triumph, in B major
stops.happening: The [[recapitulation|recapitulation]] starts with Theme 2, not Theme 1

stops.hear: The cello in fast octaves, [[double-stop|double stop]]s and runs

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: The orchestra blazes out Theme 1 one last time

notice: Listen for how late the cello enters. The orchestra has almost four minutes to itself first.
When the recapitulation arrives, notice which theme comes back first. Dvořák skips the brooding opening tune and brings back the horn tune in full glory.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Mstislav Rostropovich recorded the concerto with Herbert von Karajan and the Berlin Philharmonic in September 1968. Rostropovich is generous with time, so the movements run long. On the Spotify album the concerto is tracks 1–3, followed by Tchaikovsky’s *Variations on a Rococo Theme*.

movements.heading: Adagio, ma non troppo
movements.summary: A slow movement in G major that begins like a gentle pastoral song in the woodwinds. A sudden outburst leads to a sadder melody in the minor, taken from Dvořák’s song “Leave Me Alone”. After the calm returns, the cello plays a long, free passage of its own and the movement ends very softly.

mainIdeas.name: The pastoral song
mainIdeas.description: a gentle melody in the woodwinds, led by the clarinet.

mainIdeas.name: The song quotation
mainIdeas.description: a longing, sad melody in the minor, from “Leave Me Alone”.

stops.hear: A clarinet, with oboe and bassoon, plays a gentle melody
The cello takes up the melody and continues it
A sudden loud outburst in the orchestra, in the minor
The cello sings a longing, sad melody
stops.happening: The quotation from Dvořák’s song “Leave Me Alone”

stops.hear: Three horns play the opening melody quietly, like a hymn
stops.happening: The main theme returns, as a [[chorale|chorale]] for horns

stops.hear: The cello alone, almost free in time, with woodwinds answering; it plays chords while plucking open strings with its left hand
stops.happening: The passage most like a [[cadenza|cadenza]] in the whole concerto

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: The cello plays very soft, high, glassy notes and the movement fades

notice: In the middle section, listen to the shape of the cello’s melody: it is a song, with phrases the length of a breath. Dvořák is quoting his own vocal music.

movements.heading: Finale: Allegro moderato – Andante – Allegro vivo
movements.tempo: Finale: Allegro moderato – Andante – Allegro vivo
movements.summary: The horns start a quiet march that gathers force until the cello enters with the main tune. The tune keeps returning between contrasting episodes. Near the end the music slows almost to a standstill, memories of the first movement and of the song drift past, and then the orchestra ends the concerto stormily.

mainIdeas.name: The march tune
mainIdeas.description: a bold, dancing theme, first hinted at by the horns and then played in full by the cello.

mainIdeas.name: The farewell
mainIdeas.description: a slow, fading passage near the end that recalls earlier themes.

stops.hear: Horns play a quiet, march-like tune over low strings; it grows louder
stops.happening: The main theme, still in the distance

stops.hear: The cello enters with the full tune, bold and dancing
A sadder melody in the cello, which dissolves into quick, rippling notes in D major
The march tune returns in the orchestra
The sad melody returns, but the cello leads the music into a warmer G major, with something of the slow movement’s mood
The march tune once more
Everything slows into B major; the cello plays a tender duet with a solo violin from the orchestra
The woodwinds quietly recall the opening theme of the first movement; the cello’s line keeps falling
stops.happening: Memories of earlier music, part of the ending Dvořák rewrote after Josefina’s death

stops.label: Last 40 seconds
stops.hear: A sudden rise; the orchestra ends the concerto loudly and fast

notice: In the last minutes, listen for the first movement’s opening tune in the woodwinds. It is the concerto looking back before it ends.

threads.title: Homesickness
threads.body: Written in New York by a composer who longed for home. Unlike the *New World* Symphony, it shows few clear American influences.

threads.title: A private story
threads.body: The slow movement and the end of the finale carry the memory of Josefina, through a song she loved.

threads.title: The cello as a singer
threads.body: Dvořák, who doubted the cello as a soloist, gives it one long melody after another.

threads.title: No cadenza
threads.body: Dvořák refused one. The nearest thing is a free, songlike passage for the cello in the slow movement.

recordings.label: EMI (His Master's Voice); now Warner Classics
